html:
Argentine writer of short stories, essays and poems, one of the most influential authors of the 20th century. Born in Buenos Aires, he grew up reading English as well as Spanish and spent his teens in Geneva and Spain.

His fame rests on two story collections, Ficciones (1944) and The Aleph (1949). Short and dense, the stories play with ideas: a library holding every possible book, a garden of forking paths where time branches, a world invented by a secret society that starts to replace our own. Labyrinths, mirrors and infinity run through them.

He was a fierce opponent of Juan Perón, whose government removed him from his library job in 1946. After Perón's fall he became director of the National Library in 1955, just as he was going blind.

International fame came in the 1960s, when he shared a major prize with Samuel Beckett and his work was translated widely. He never won the Nobel Prize. His games with fiction shaped later writers across the world, including the Latin American boom of Gabriel García Márquez. He died in Geneva in 1986.
